newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Canada seeks legally-binding agreement on forests.
newsitem.headline: Canada seeks legally-binding agreement on forests.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien on Tuesday expressed alarm over the decline of the world's forests and called for a strong, legally-binding agreement to preserve them.
"The forests of the world continue to decline at an alarming rate. Sustainable forest management is a high Canadian priority," he told the U.N. Earth Summit.

"We are convinced that this special session presents a unique opportunity to achieve an international forest convention through the creation of an intergovernmental negotiation committee," said Chretien. Canada has about 10 percent of the world's forests.
"Our country believes that a strong, legally-binding agreement...is the best way to ensure the international will needed to reverse the tide of deforestation," he said.
A convention would also help Canada achieve its own forest management goals.
Many environmentalists oppose an international forest convention, fearing it would take years to negotiate and be ratified and end up by formalising weak, non-binding standards.
While the European Union, Malaysia and Russia are among countries favouring a convention, the United States, Brazil, India and Australia are opposed.

They say better alternatives might include a follow-up to a U.N.-created Intergovernmental Panel on Forests that has made over 1,000 proposals, or action through existing treaties such as those on climate change and biological diversity.
